newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire reinforces as rebels extend Shaba push.
newsitem.headline: Zaire reinforces as rebels extend Shaba push.

text.p: Rebels have extended their push into Zaire's mineral- producing Shaba province, after countering the army's much-trumpeted offensive by opening a new front, sources on both sides say.

But the government in Kinshasa, brushing aside repeated rebel offers of talks, was reinforcing by train from the provincial capital Lubumbashi and a second military base at Kamina, a Zairean defence official told Reuters.
Foreign mercenaries, many of them from former Yugoslavia, remained deployed much further north at the airport serving the rebel-held town of Watsa, said the official, who asked not to be named.

"We didn't have many troops in Kalemie. It was our strategy to go further to the north," he said, referring to the strategic Shaba province lakeside town which the army earlier admitted losing on Monday.
"They had us, but we are sending in reinforcements by train," he added.
The Tutsi-led rebels launched their campaign in October, accusing the Zairean authorities of denying them citizenship and seeking to return them to Rwanda, which their forebears left generations ago.
The army, its leadership reshuffled as was the government by veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko in December, launched its counter-offensive on January 20.

It failed to dislodge the rebels from towns and territory along the borders with Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi and the rebels hit back on several fronts, latterly targeting Kalemie and pressing on towards Moba, 150 km (90 miles) away.

While both are hundreds of km (miles) from the copper and cobalt mines around Lubumbashi, the two towns are key transport hubs on Lake Tanganyika. Kalemie, with its port and airport, has links to the whole Shaba region.
As the front lines have shifted, Zaire has taken its case to the international stage, accusing neighbouring Rwanda and Uganda of invading and fighting alongside the rebels.
On Tuesday, it urged teenagers to enlist in the army as part of a fresh mobilisation drive. The call met with a mixed reception among teenagers on the streets of the sprawling capital.

Mobutu, who returned to Europe for further medical tests after prostate surgery in August and one prolonged absence, on Tuesday visited Morocco, which intervened to help crush a 1970s revolt in Shaba.
Aides said that the veteran leader, who seized power in 1965, would return to Zaire this week.
Togo and Egypt have rejected suggestions from officials in Kinshasa that they might send troops or material to help the army regain the initiative.
Morocco and Chad, like Togo said to be ready to help fight the rebels, have remained silent on the suggestions.
Earlier, Zaire's Deputy Foreign Minister Henri-Thomas Lokondo Yoka ruled out talks despite the latest setbacks. "They may be winning battles but they have not won the war," he told Reuters.
